title: The Morning Brief: Military escalation and trade war reshape global markets
dek: Wednesday brought military strikes in the Middle East, diplomatic expulsions in Europe, and tariff threats against Canada, while domestic courts blocked voting restrictions and affirmed ethics rules. Oil crossed $100 a barrel amid US-Iran escalation.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: Geopolitical and trade tensions are driving energy costs sharply higher and reshaping diplomatic alignments, while US courts continue to constrain the administration's election and data-sharing policies.
bottom_line: Military strikes in the Gulf, diplomatic expulsions in Europe, and tariff threats against Canada created a single arc of escalation Wednesday that pushed oil above $100 a barrel and reshaped strategic alignments. US courts blocked voting restrictions and affirmed ethics constraints on the administration. The calendar brings Supreme Court decisions on mail ballots and IRS data-sharing, continued military exchanges in the Strait of Hormuz, and Russia's response to Hungary's expulsion of diplomats.
body: The morning's dominant thread is escalation: military strikes in the Middle East and Red Sea, diplomatic expulsions in Europe, and trade weaponry deployed against Canada have created a cascade of instability that is pricing directly into global oil markets and reshaping alliances.

In the Gulf, US and Iranian forces traded strikes through September 8 and 9. The US military destroyed multiple Iranian tankers in the Gulf of Oman after Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps targeted a US Navy warship with ballistic missiles. Neither attack resulted in US casualties, the warship evaded the Iranian strikes, but the tit-for-tat exchange has pushed Brent crude above $100 a barrel for the first time in months. Oil rose 2.7 percent to about $100.6 a barrel on Wednesday, marking the third time Brent has crossed $100 this year and reflecting a more than 60 percent gain since January. The Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of global oil passes, has seen shipping volumes decline sharply from the direct attacks on tankers and infrastructure. The spike translates immediately to American households: gasoline averaged $4.15 per gallon on Monday, up 7 cents from the prior week and 39 percent since February when the US and Israel first struck Iran. Diesel hit $5.90 per gallon, matching all-time highs.

In Europe, Hungary's Foreign Minister Anita Orbán ordered 10 Russian diplomats to leave Budapest on September 8, a sharp reversal from Hungary's historical alignment with Moscow. The expulsion comes under Hungary's new government, elected in April 2026, which has formally declared Russia a threat to Hungarian security and to the Hungarian minority in Ukraine. This marks a geopolitical realignment that stands as Hungary's most significant policy pivot in years; Russia's response, whether reciprocal expulsion or escalation, will determine the trajectory of bilateral relations.

On trade, President Trump escalated conflict with Canada by directing the General Services Administration to remove Canadian products from federal contracting schedules worth more than $50 billion annually. The order directly targets Bombardier, Canada's major aerospace manufacturer, which employs over 1,400 workers in Wichita, Kansas. Bombardier's supply chain extends to about 2,800 US companies across 47 states, creating political complications in a state Trump won decisively. Canada retaliated the same day with tariffs on about $20 billion of US goods, including defense procurement where Canada is reconsidering its plan to purchase US F-35 fighter jets and has received a proposal from Swedish defense contractor Saab to manufacture the Gripen jet in Canada instead.

Domestic courts continued to constrain administration policies. The US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia upheld an injunction Wednesday blocking the IRS from sharing taxpayer information with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The three-judge panel ruled the Trump administration's data-sharing policy violated federal tax-confidentiality law by allowing ICE to bulk-request addresses of 1.28 million suspected undocumented immigrants without meeting legal safeguards. The IRS had already shared 47,289 taxpayer records with ICE before the lower-court block took effect; those records remain in ICE custody while the program is halted prospectively. On voting, Justice Brett Kavanaugh rejected an emergency appeal from Missouri Republicans seeking to use a newly drawn congressional map for the November 2026 midterms. The decision preserved a Missouri Supreme Court ruling that upheld a voter referendum blocking the map, leaving the 2022 configuration with six Republican and two Democratic seats in place. The Trump administration also filed its third emergency Supreme Court appeal Sunday seeking to reinstate a USPS rule that would restrict mail-in ballots. U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani blocked the rule on September 5, finding it would "threaten disenfranchisement of millions" less than seventy days before the election. The USPS rule would allow the postal service to track mail-in ballots and potentially reject ballots sent to voters not included in a federal database. The Supreme Court must decide whether to grant the emergency stay before Alabama and other states complete ballot mailing processes beginning September 9.

Other developments: A Boeing 767 operated by 21 Air crashed at Miami International Airport on September 6, killing five people after landing at approximately 185 mph and overrunning the runway by 1,300 feet. NTSB investigators are examining whether runway safety infrastructure could have prevented the overflight. The Houthis launched coordinated drone and ballistic missile attacks across southern Saudi Arabia on September 8, wounding 73 people and igniting fires at oil facilities and utilities, marking the most serious escalation since a UN-brokered truce in 2022. Hurricane Lowell knocked out power to nearly all members of the Kauai island utility cooperative on September 8, leaving about 50,400 customers without power statewide. Iceland summoned the US ambassador on September 8 after President Trump posted a map on Truth Social depicting Iceland, Canada, Greenland, Mexico, and other territories covered by the US flag. Iceland's Foreign Minister called the image "completely inappropriate." King Charles III issued a formal letter on September 7 confirming Prince Harry and Meghan remain non-working members of the royal family following their return to Britain from California. Jaguar Land Rover announced September 7 that it will cut 4,000 jobs over the next two years as it attempts to save £1.7 billion, with most cuts affecting the UK head office; the company's sales slumped by a fifth to £22.9 billion from £29 billion over the previous two years, with US tariffs and a cyberattack cited as main causes. LIV Golf filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on September 8 after Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund withdrew funding; the tour plans to restart in early 2027 under new investor BC Partners. Russia and North Korea opened the first direct road bridge connecting their border on September 8, spanning the Tumen River and able to accommodate up to 300 vehicles and 2,323 people daily. New Hampshire held primary elections on September 8 for Senate, House, and gubernatorial seats. Financial disclosure forms show Trump distributed $45,000 in cash as holiday gifts to three White House staff members and $20,000 to a fourth, representing roughly one-third of the recipients' annual salaries; legal experts cited in reporting say the payments may violate federal law.
